newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Tenor Vince Gill - Country Music's "Mr. Nice Guy".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tenor Vince Gill - Country Music's "Mr. Nice Guy".

text.p: He's won 10 Grammys, been named the U.S. Country Music Association's Entertainer of the Year twice, and collected more country music awards than any other performer.
Add to that a shelf full of awards from other country music groups and here's Vince Gill -- nice guy, modest and unassuming, so ... well ... normal.

He refers to himself with aw-shucks modesty as a "boy singer," but he's proud and a bit bemused, at his age -- just shy of 40 -- at having recently been given a Lifetime Achievement Award by Gibson Musical Instruments "for outstanding contributions to the world of guitar."
And there's his ever-present good-guy persona. He regularly plays at charity benefits and was last year named the BMI music publishers "Humanitarian of the Year."

An Oklahoman, he staged a benefit concert after the 1995 bombing of the Oklahoma City federal building that killed 168 people, and was invited back to raise the flag to full-staff at the end of the mourning period.

Why involved with so many benefits? "I think it makes sense," he told Reuters in a recent interview. "No matter how good you've got it, or how bad, there's somebody who's less fortunate than you. If they need time to do something, I'd rather give of my time. I think it means more than to just write a check.
NO FRILLS PERFORMER
On the concert stage, Gill goes the no-frills route, shunning the cowboy hats, fringed leather jackets, tight jeans and spangled shirts that are part of the popular caricature of country music stars.
At a recent sold-out concert at an arena outside Washington he wore loose, faded denims, a white T-shirt and an unbuttoned plaid flannel shirt. No cowboy hat -- he doesn't even own one.

From his attire, he might have just come from the golf course -- since Gill's second passion after music is golf. He considered becoming a professional golfer, and Gill says his lifetime ambition is to win the Masters.

But it was his phenomenal musical talent that brought almost 14,000 fans to the arena. After nearly an hour's warm-up concert by new country singer Bryan White, also an Oklahoman, Gill rewarded them with 2-1/2 hours of heart-rending and heart-mending ballads, rowdy rockers, cool blues and jazzy bluegrass.
Gill doesn't hold with much stage patter. "I don't talk much," he told the crowd. "That gives me more time to play and sing."
Many of the lyrics, delivered in Gill's flawless tenor, sprang from his own pen.

The audience screamed with delight when they recognised the keyboards opening to "When I Call Your Name," (that won Gill his first Grammy in 1990) and applauded lustily for "Never Knew Lonely Till You" ("My momma's favourite," said Gill) and "Tryin' to Get Over You."
Gill's been playing guitar since he was five years old. He grew up in Oklahoma City, where his father, a lawyer who later became a federal judge, played banjo in his spare time.
"I started with a little bitty guitar," Gill said. He also plays fiddle and other stringed instruments. "I don't know if I ever played it as much as I just carried it around."
ONE POP HIT RECORD

He formed a high school bluegrass band, made a short detour into pop, with one hit record ("Let Me Love You Tonight," with Pure Prairie League), then moved to Nashville as a session musician famed for his guitar licks before hitting it big in mainstream country.

Chet Atkins was a childhood hero, and he listened to Patsy Cline and Jim Reeves records, as well as the blues his older brother favoured. Gill's gospel-flavored elegy to that brother, who died last year, "Go Rest High on that Mountain," won him a Grammy in 1995.

His latest two Grammys, announced last month, were for a song about reconciliation, "Worlds Apart," and for a bluegrass collaboration with Alison Krauss and Union Station for "High Lonesome Sound," the title song from his current album, a wide-ranging whing-ding of musical styles.
For his current Kraft Foods-sponsored tour, which also benefits a feed-the-hungry programme called Second Harvest, Gill will spend 85 weekends on the road with his band.
His 16-year-old daughter Jenny plans to join him for some summer dates. "We're touring with Bryan White," he said. "She thinks he's pretty cute."
